title: A linear autoencoder is PCA
objectives: Show that a trained linear autoencoder spans the top principal components.

screens.title: Where will it point?
screens.prose: These are `eigen` l11's ten days of two stocks, demeaned, with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2\\2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. We train a linear autoencoder with **one** code on 2,000 days drawn with this covariance. Its encoder is one column, a direction in the plane.
screens.question: Drag the handle to where you predict the trained encoder's direction points.

hints.text: A one-number code should keep as much of each day as it can.
Which direction did `eigen` l11 find for the widest spread?
PC1 is $(2, 1)/\sqrt5$; at radius 3 that is $(2.68, 1.34)$.

feedback.correct: The trained encoder points along the data's own PC1, close to $(2, 1)/\sqrt5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about which line loses the least of each day.

byKey.axis: Along stock A alone, the code would drop all of B's own moves. The trained direction tilts up.
byKey.diag: The diagonal treats the stocks alike, but A varies more (5 against 2). The trained direction leans towards A.

explain.text: The trained encoder column, normalised, is $(0.902, 0.432)$: the PC1 of the 2,000 days to within 0.001 degrees, near $(2, 1)/\sqrt5 \approx (0.894, 0.447)$. Training found the principal component without being told about eigenvectors.

screens.title: The error it reaches
screens.prose: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ has eigenvalues 6 and 1. The autoencoder's error settled at 1.0015; the 2,000 days' own covariance, divided by $n$, has eigenvalues 5.9418 and 1.0015.
screens.question: For data with exactly this $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, what error does the best one-code linear autoencoder reach?

hints.text: The code keeps one direction. What is left over?
The variance across PC1 is the smaller eigenvalue.

feedback.correct: 1: the variance along PC2, the direction the code drops.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which eigenvalue belongs to the direction the code cannot keep?

byKey.kept: 6 is the variance the code keeps, along PC1. The error is what it loses.
byKey.total: 7 is the total variance. The code keeps 6 of it.

explain.text: The code keeps PC1 and loses PC2, whose variance is the smaller eigenvalue, 1. The trained 1.0015 matches the sample's own smaller eigenvalue, 1.0015, to many places.

screens.title: The share it keeps
screens.prose: The total variance is $6 + 1 = 7$, the trace of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. The one-code autoencoder keeps the variance along PC1.
screens.question: What share of the variance does it keep? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Kept over total.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the kept variance by the total.

byKey.lost: That is the share lost. The question asks what is kept.
byKey.ratio: You divided dropped by kept. Divide kept by the total, 7.

explain.text: It keeps $6/7 \approx 85.7\%$ and loses the rest, which is exactly its error of 1 out of 7.

screens.title: Two codes from three
screens.prose: Three stocks have a covariance with eigenvalues 5, 2 and 0.5. A linear autoencoder keeps the top $k$ principal directions; its error is the sum of the eigenvalues it drops.
screens.question: What is the error of the best linear autoencoder with 2 codes?

hints.text: Two codes keep the two largest.
Only $\lambda_3$ is dropped.

feedback.correct: 0.5: only the smallest eigenvalue is dropped.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the eigenvalues the code drops.

byKey.one: 2.5 is the error with one code, $2 + 0.5$. Two codes also keep $\lambda_2$.
byKey.kept: 7 is what two codes keep. The error is what is left.

explain.text: Two codes keep 5 and 2 and drop 0.5, so the error is 0.5. With one code it would be $2 + 0.5 = 2.5$.

screens.title: Is it the eigenvector?
screens.prose: Two runs on the same days start from different random sizes. Run A ends with encoder $(0.91, 0.44)$ and decoder $(0.89, 0.43)$. Run B ends with $(0.66, 0.31)$ and $(1.24, 0.59)$. Both reach the error 1.0015.
screens.question: Which reading is right?

options.text: Both point along PC1; only the product of encoder and decoder is fixed, not their lengths
Run B failed, since a trained encoder should be the unit eigenvector
options.why: Run B reaches the same error. Its encoder has length 0.73, and its decoder 1.38 makes up for it.

options.text: Both failed, since trained weights should be orthonormal like PCA's
options.why: Nothing in the loss asks for unit length. Any length works if the decoder divides it back out.

options.text: Run B found a different direction from run A
options.why: Both columns lie on the same line through the origin. Only their lengths differ.

hints.text: Compare the directions, then the lengths.
Run B's encoder is 0.73 long and its decoder 1.38; multiply.

feedback.correct: Right. The loss fixes $\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$, the projection onto PC1, not each factor.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the error first, then the directions.

byKey.fail: You expected the eigenvector itself. The loss cannot tell a long encoder with a short decoder from a unit pair.
byKey.orth: You expected PCA's unit columns. Training has no reason to produce them.

explain.text: Encoder length times decoder length is about 1 in both runs (1.00 and 1.00). With more codes, any invertible mixing $\mathbf{A}$ of the codes, undone by $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ in the decoder, gives the same rebuild: only the subspace is fixed.

screens.title: Mixing the codes
screens.prose: A two-code autoencoder on three stocks has encoder $\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}$ ($3 \times 2$) and decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$ ($2 \times 3$). We replace the encoder by $\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}\mathbf{A}$ with $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
screens.question: Which decoder rebuilds every day exactly as before?

options.text: $\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$
$\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$, unchanged
options.why: The codes are now mixed by $\mathbf{A}$. An unchanged decoder reads them wrongly.

options.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$
options.why: That mixes a second time. The decoder must undo $\mathbf{A}$.

options.text: $\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$
options.why: $\mathbf{A}$ is not a rotation, so its transpose does not undo it.

hints.text: The rebuild is $\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{D}$ for the new decoder $\mathbf{D}$.
You need $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The new decoder must undo $\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: Since $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{I}$, the product and so the error are unchanged. The two new codes are mixtures of the old ones, so a single code has no fixed meaning.

screens.title: No favourite direction
screens.prose: Now $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = 2\mathbf{I}$, `eigen` l11's round cloud: every direction has variance 2. We draw three samples of 2,000 days and train a one-code autoencoder on each. The encoders point at 130, 3 and 25 degrees.
screens.question: What decides each direction?

options.text: Each sample's own noise: the population has no preferred direction
The random start of the weights, which differed between runs
options.why: We kept the same start for all three. The days differed, and so did the directions.

options.text: A bug in training, since all three runs should agree
options.why: With equal eigenvalues every direction is equally good, so nothing makes them agree.

options.text: The axes, since training prefers stock A's direction
options.why: The directions are spread around. The loss has no favourite axis.

hints.text: With $2\mathbf{I}$, how much variance does each direction carry?
Each sample's covariance is a little off $2\mathbf{I}$ by chance.

feedback.correct: Right. Each sample's small chance tilt picks the direction.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what differs between the three runs.

explain.text: Every direction keeps variance 2, so every run's error is close to 2 (1.949, 1.967, 1.970). The direction follows each sample's chance tilt, so reading meaning into it is a mistake.

screens.title: Why the dropped eigenvalues
screens.prose: Take centred data with covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf{v}_i\mathbf{v}_i^\top$, and keep the top $k$ eigenvectors. Then: $$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}} &= \textstyle\sum_{i > k} (\mathbf{v}_i^\top\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{v}_i \\ \mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2 &= \textstyle\sum_{i > k} \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{v}_i^\top\mathbf{x})^2] \\ &= \;?\end{aligned}$$
screens.question: Which line completes the derivation?

options.text: $\sum_{i > k} \mathbf{v}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_{i > k}\lambda_i$
$\sum_{i \le k} \mathbf{v}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_{i \le k}\lambda_i$
options.why: That sums the kept directions. The residual lives on the dropped ones, $i > k$.

options.text: $\sum_{i > k} (\mathbf{v}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}_i)^2 = \sum_{i > k}\lambda_i^2$
$\sum_{i > k} \sqrt{\mathbf{v}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}_i} = \sum_{i > k}\sqrt{\lambda_i}$
options.why: The square root would give a standard deviation. The error is a variance.

hints.text: For centred $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{x})^2] = \mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}$.
For an eigenvector, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\mathbf{v}_i^\top\mathbf{v}_i = 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. Each dropped coordinate contributes its variance, $\lambda_i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What is the variance of the coordinate $\mathbf{v}_i^\top\mathbf{x}$?

explain.text: The residual keeps the dropped coordinates, which are uncorrelated with mean 0. Each squared coordinate averages $\mathbf{v}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}_i = \lambda_i$, so the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues; no linear map with $k$ codes does better (`eigen` l10).

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
# train_autoencoder (l5), pca_recon_error and subspace_angle
# are defined for you.


def check_pca(X, k, steps, lr, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    W_enc, W_dec = train_autoencoder(X, k, steps, lr, seed)
    Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    trained = float(((Xc @ W_enc @ W_dec - Xc) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean())
    lam, V = np.linalg.eigh(Xc.T @ Xc / len(Xc))
    top = V[:, ::-1][:, :k]
    return trained, pca_recon_error(X, k), subspace_angle(W_enc, top)
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step


def train_autoencoder(X, k, steps, lr, seed):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    X = X - X.mean(axis=0)              # centre each column
    n, d = X.shape
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W_enc = Tensor(0.1 * g.standard_normal((d, k)))
    W_dec = Tensor(0.1 * g.standard_normal((k, d)))
    params = [W_enc, W_dec]
    m = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p.data) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        for p in params:
            p.zero_grad()
        D = X @ W_enc @ W_dec - X
        loss = (D ** 2).sum() / n
        loss.backward()
        new, m, v = adam_step([p.data for p in params], [p.grad for p in params], m, v, t, lr)
        for p, q in zip(params, new):
            p.data = q
    return W_enc.data, W_dec.data




def pca_recon_error(X, k):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    X = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X / len(X))     # ascending
    return float(lam[:len(lam) - k].sum())


def subspace_angle(W, V):
    Qw = np.linalg.qr(np.asarray(W, dtype=float))[0]
    Qv = np.linalg.qr(np.asarray(V, dtype=float))[0]
    s = np.linalg.svd(Qw.T @ Qv, compute_uv=False)
    return float(np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(s.min(), -1.0, 1.0))))

screens.title: Factors from a risk model
screens.prose: A risk team builds statistical factors from PCA on 300 stocks. A colleague proposes a linear autoencoder with the same number of codes, trained with Adam, as the modern replacement.
screens.question: What would it give them?

options.text: The same factor space as PCA, with codes mixed by an arbitrary invertible map
A better fit, since training finds what PCA misses
options.why: For squared error and a linear model, PCA is already the best fit. Training can only match it.

options.text: Factors with clearer meaning, such as one per sector
options.why: Any invertible mixing fits equally well, so the codes come with no fixed meaning at all.

options.text: A worse fit, since gradient descent stops early
options.why: Run long enough it reaches the closed form, as our 2,000 days showed. The issue is that it adds nothing.

hints.text: What is the best linear map with $k$ codes?
What does training fix, and what does it leave free?

feedback.correct: Right. A linear autoencoder adds nothing until it is nonlinear.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall what the best linear autoencoder spans.

byKey.better: You expected training to beat PCA. For a linear model and squared error nothing can.
byKey.named: You expected meaningful codes. Only the subspace is fixed.

explain.text: A linear autoencoder spans the top principal components, so it reproduces the PCA factor space and no more. A nonlinear one is where something new can happen, in the next lesson.

ideas: For centred data and squared error, the best linear autoencoder with $k$ codes spans the top $k$ principal components.
Its error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues: 1 for $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2\\2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, keeping $6/7$ of the variance.
Only the subspace is fixed: any invertible mixing of the codes, undone by the decoder, fits as well, so trained weights need not be unit or orthogonal.

formula.name: Best linear error
formula.note: Eigenvalues of the covariance with $1/n$, in decreasing order.

summary.trap: Expecting the trained encoder to equal the unit eigenvector: only its span is fixed.
